solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Horrified – part of Reichstag has termites!

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is wanted, a run of letters spanning them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the building, the verb and the start of the insects

explanation.surface: Someone is appalled to discover that the German parliament building is infested with wood-eating insects.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles three words: reichstAG HAS Termites. The dash and exclamation mark make the whole thing read as a shocked outburst.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone horrified is filled with dismay and shock; the two words are straightforward synonyms describing an appalled state.

clue.text: Ad hoc social media group: “keep it quiet; Farah’s putting on weight”

blocks.note: flab is the extra body weight someone puts on
sh! is the call to keep quiet
Mo Farah, the British Olympic distance runner

explanation.surface: A runner is told to keep quiet about gaining a few pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Mo Farah is a famous British Olympic long-distance runner, so 'Farah' gives his first name; 'weight' is the body fat he has put on, not a unit.
explanation.definitionFit: A flash mob is a crowd summoned through online networks to gather suddenly, perform briefly and then disperse.

clue.text: Vacations at sea taking in Ontario’s premier island

indicators.note: the premier of anything is its first, so only the opening letter of the province is kept
the holidays take in the extra letter, absorbing it into the pile of letters
something at sea is confused and adrift, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as printed, anagram fodder
the first letter of the Canadian province

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers on a cruise take in the top island of a Canadian province.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten letters from VACATIONS plus O are rearranged. 'Premier' tempts as a political leader, but here it only means first letter. The province includes Cape Breton Island, and the mainland part is nearly surrounded by sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canadian maritime province is loosely called an island: its peninsula is almost cut off by water and it includes Cape Breton Island.

clue.text: Constant sport, to put the icing on the cake!

definitions.text: put the icing on the cake

blocks.note: pi is the mathematical constant, about 3.14
PE is physical education, school sport

explanation.surface: A pastry chef lists the finishing touches for a cake: a constant, some sport, then the icing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put the icing on the cake' reads as the idiom for a final flourish, but here it is literal: squeezing icing through a nozzle onto a cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Bakers decorate a cake by forcing icing through a bag and nozzle, which is exactly what piping means in the kitchen.

clue.text: Whisks off Best, 21, missing the second part

indicators.note: the two-word answer at 21 drops its second word, so only the first stays
something that has gone off is spoilt and out of shape, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as printed, anagram fodder
the answer to 21 across without its second word

explanation.surface: Someone whisks away the footballer George Best while a reference to another clue sits oddly in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 across is REGGAE MUSIC; drop MUSIC and mix REGGAE with BEST. 'Whisks' looks like a verb meaning snatches away, but it is the plural noun, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisks and egg beaters are both kitchen tools for rapidly stirring air into eggs or cream; the terms are synonyms.

clue.text: Germany and Spain failing to respect Arab ruler

indicators.note: the two countries fail to appear in the verb that follows, so their letters drop out of it

blocks.note: to admire someone is to respect them
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: Two European nations are accused of showing too little regard for a Middle Eastern leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove D and E from ADMIRE: A(D)MIR(E). The surface wants 'failing to respect' as one phrase, but 'respect' is the word losing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An amir, also spelt emir, is a Muslim prince, commander or governor, especially one heading an Arab state.

clue.text: Amateur Jack Rooney announced as a seed

indicators.note: announcing is saying out loud, so the footballer's first name is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for amateur
J is jack in a pack of cards
Wayne Rooney, the England footballer; a wain is a farm wagon

explanation.surface: An unpaid player named Jack Rooney is announced as a seeded entrant in a tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seed' pretends to mean a ranked tennis entrant; it is literal. WAIN, an old word for a cart, is spelt differently from the footballer's name but sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Ajwain, also called carom, is a small aromatic spice from India, used whole in curries and breads like caraway.

clue.text: Mail intended reporting weapons

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so the two synonyms are to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: chain mail is armour
what you intended is what you meant

explanation.surface: Letters sent through the post are said to have been aimed at weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mail' looks like post but is chain mail. Said with a British accent that drops the final R, ARMOUR MEANT runs together as ARMAMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Armament is the collective term for a military force's guns and other arms, so it serves as a synonym.

clue.text: It’s exasperating getting hold of operator when flying

blocks.note: something galling is exasperating
the word cut short to its first two letters, the clipped form used for camera operators

explanation.surface: A frustrated caller complains about trying to reach a telephone operator while on a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying' looks like air travel, but it means going very fast, as in galloping inflation; 'when' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something galloping, like galloping inflation, is moving or increasing at great speed, just as something flying is rushing along.

clue.text: Officer to harm little woman in custody

indicators.note: someone in custody is held by another

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil or harm
Jo March, one of the sisters in Little Women

explanation.surface: A police officer is accused of hurting a small woman held in a cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' is a nod to Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women, whose heroine is Jo March; 'Officer' is army, not police.
explanation.definitionFit: A major is a commissioned army rank above captain, so the answer is one kind of military officer.

clue.text: Pacify ace German mathematician returning to base

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came

blocks.note: A is ace on playing cards
Carl Friedrich Gauss, the German mathematician
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A brilliant German mathematician heads back to headquarters to calm things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a military home, but it is the mathematical constant e, fitting the mathematician theme; 'to' just joins it on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To assuage anger or grief is to soothe and calm it, which is what pacifying someone does; the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Bush to stop Arab travelling west

indicators.note: across entries read west to east, so heading west means the word runs backwards

blocks.note: to bar someone is to stop them
taken as printed

explanation.surface: A politician moves to block a Middle Eastern traveller heading westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' reads as the American president, or a shrub, but it is his wife: Barbara Bush, First Lady and mother of another president.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbara Bush was the wife of President George H. W. Bush, so she is one famous person with that surname.

clue.text: Cat starts to torment old Macavity

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their first letters, the only ones kept

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A cat sets about tormenting Macavity, the villainous feline from T. S. Eliot's poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Macavity, the Mystery Cat of Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, keeps the whole surface feline.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, so the answer is a particular kind of the animal named by the definition.

clue.text: Body knight buried in old north- east French citadel

indicators.note: something buried lies inside what covers it

blocks.note: a carcass is a dead body
O is the standard abbreviation for old
N is the knight in chess notation
NE is the compass abbreviation for north-east

explanation.surface: A knight's corpse lies entombed in an ancient fortress in north-eastern France.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface tempts you to look in north-east France, but the compass points are only letters: the walled city is in the far south.
explanation.definitionFit: Carcassonne is a walled hilltop city in southern France, famous for its restored medieval fortifications, so it is a citadel.

clue.text: Kray, with terrible ailment relating to military manouevres

indicators.note: a terrible state is a mess, so the illness is scrambled

blocks.note: Reggie Kray, one of the notorious London gangster twins
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A notorious gangster with a nasty illness gets tied up in army exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kray twins, Reggie and Ronnie, were 1960s East End London gangsters; this clue takes Reg, and 25 across takes Ron.
explanation.definitionFit: Regimental describes things belonging to an army regiment, so it covers matters of military units and their drills.

clue.text: Featured in Australian commonly, Syd Cohen’s regularly taken poison

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the name is kept
a thing featured in another appears within it, so the chosen letters sit inside the dialect

blocks.note: Strine is the popular name for broad Australian speech
the even-numbered letters of SYD COHEN

explanation.surface: An Australian character called Syd Cohen is often seen taking poison.
explanation.walkthrough: Strine is Australian English as it sounds in everyday speech, itself a slurred 'Australian'. 'Commonly' marks it as the vernacular, not an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Strychnine is a highly toxic alkaloid from plant seeds, once used to kill rats, and a classic fictional murder weapon.

clue.text: Tobias returned, missing one shoe

indicators.note: the name is returned the way it came, so it reads backwards
the numeral for one goes missing, so that letter drops out

blocks.note: taken as printed
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A man called Tobias came back without one of his shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: TOBIAS backwards is SAIBOT; take out I to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabot is a wooden clog, worn by peasants in France and elsewhere, so it is a type of footwear.

clue.text: Copper despatched to seize criminal gear

indicators.note: criminal means crooked, so the equipment's letters are bent out of order
to seize something is to grab it

blocks.note: despatched means sent off
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A police officer is sent out to confiscate stolen equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is British informal for a police officer, not the metal, and 'criminal' works on the word after it rather than describing the gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a police rank above constable, so the answer is one kind of copper, the slang for police officer.

clue.text: Blimey, hotel runs out of clarified butter

blocks.note: ghee is the clarified butter of Indian cooking
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A cook exclaims in surprise when the hotel kitchen runs out of ghee.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove H from GHEE. Blimey is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild interjections of astonishment, the British one and its American counterpart, so they are interchangeable exclamations.

clue.text: Criticise Sunday lunch?

blocks.note: to pan or savage someone's work harshly, often mockingly
the traditional British weekend meal of a joint of meat cooked in the oven

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Sunday lunch is only one example of the second sense. In Britain the Sunday roast is a traditional family meal of roast meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast is slang for harsh mockery, and a roast is the joint of meat served at the weekly family meal.

clue.text: Aero Bar melted, left in sylvan setting

blocks.note: an Aero is a British chocolate bar full of bubbles; anagram fodder
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A chocolate bar has melted after being left out in a woodland spot.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aero is a bubbly British chocolate bar. 'Left in' reads as abandoned, but L simply joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Arboreal means relating to or living among trees, and sylvan means wooded, so both evoke a forest environment.

clue.text: Cue Aggers – I’m broadcasting score from the West Indies

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters things widely, so these letters are thrown into new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator is cued to give the score of a match against the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: Aggers is Jonathan Agnew, a BBC cricket commentator. 'Score' looks like runs in cricket, but it is music.
explanation.definitionFit: Reggae is the popular music style that emerged in Jamaica in the 1960s, so it is a musical score of Caribbean origin.

clue.text: Direct navy to support Tory minister

indicators.note: in a down entry the supporting piece is underneath

blocks.note: Michael Gove, a Conservative cabinet minister
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: An order goes out for the navy to back a Conservative government minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the informal name for Britain's Conservative party, and Michael Gove served in several of its cabinets.
explanation.definitionFit: To govern is to control and steer the affairs of a country or organisation, which is to direct it.

clue.text: Mike left a fortune for another bloke

blocks.note: in British slang, a bomb is a lot of money, as in 'cost a bomb'
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Mike leaves a fortune in his will to some other fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove M from BOMB. 'Another bloke' is fair because Mike is already one; bloke is British for man.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob is a common man's first name, so it names one more male individual beyond the Mike already mentioned.

clue.text: Explosive device found in Kabul letterbomb

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the Afghan capital into the start of the second word

explanation.surface: A bomb disguised as a letter is discovered in the Afghan capital.
explanation.walkthrough: kaBUL LETterbomb. The definition is loose: a bullet is fired by an explosive charge rather than being a bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullet is a projectile driven out of a gun by an exploding charge, so it is loosely classed with munitions.

clue.text: Besiege Kray following rumour of jealousy

indicators.note: a rumour is something heard said, so the feeling is taken by its sound
the gangster comes after the other piece, so his name is placed second

blocks.note: envy is jealousy
Ronnie Kray, one of the notorious London gangster twins

explanation.surface: A gangster lays siege to someone after hearing gossip about a jealous rival.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kray twins were 1960s East End London gangsters; 15 down used Reggie, and this clue uses Ronnie.
explanation.definitionFit: To environ is to surround or encircle, which is what an army does when it besieges a town.

clue.text: Allegedly pulled a blade in the street

indicators.note: what is alleged is only said, so the verb is taken as it is spoken

blocks.note: an oar's blade is pulled through the water when rowing

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of drawing a knife in a public thoroughfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled a blade' reads as producing a knife, but the blade is the flat end of an oar.
explanation.definitionFit: A road and a street are both public ways for traffic through a town, so they are near synonyms.

clue.text: Agent Gerald stripped of military rank

indicators.note: both names are stripped of their outer layers, leaving only their insides

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters
the name without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A spy named Gerald is demoted, losing his army commission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped of military rank' reads as a demotion, but 'stripped' works on the two words before it, and 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: General is the highest army officer grade in most forces, so it is one of the ranks named by the definition.

clue.text: Donated 26 grand upfront

indicators.note: being upfront means going at the head, so the thousand is placed first

blocks.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
the answer to 26 down is ROAD, and Ave (avenue) is another road

explanation.surface: Someone handed over twenty-six thousand pounds in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' pretends to be a sum of money beside 'grand', but it points to the answer at 26 down. G goes before AVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gave is the past tense of give, and to give money to a cause is to donate it.

clue.text: Standard American opera

blocks.note: a norm is a standard
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A staple production from the American operatic repertoire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard American opera' reads as a single description, but it splits into two pieces of wordplay and then the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is Bellini's 1831 tragic work about a Druid priestess, so it is one particular opera.

clue.text: Commercial vehicle time after time making a profit

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial on TV or radio
a van is a vehicle
T is the abbreviation for time
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: A delivery van used for business works around the clock to turn a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time after time' reads as repeatedly, but it gives two separate time words, T and then AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Advantage and profit both mean benefit or gain, as in turning something to your advantage or profit.
